rule: Two kinds of line. A quote is his own recorded words and always shows its source. A companion line is the school's words in his character (congratulations, tips, the word about skipping) and shows no source. The two are never mixed in one bubble.

marcus.name: Marcus Aurelius
marcus.role: Emperor of Rome, who wrote notes to himself
marcus.credit: Marble bust, Louvre MR 561, about 170 AD. Photograph public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

greet.t: In the morning, when you are slow to get up, keep this in mind: I am rising to do the work of a human being.
Do not act as if you were going to live ten thousand years. While you live, while it is in your power, be good.
Stop talking about what a good person should be. Be one.
Look inward. Within is the fountain of good, and it will always bubble up if you keep digging.

done.t: Practise even the things you despair of. The left hand, useless at most things for want of practice, holds the reins better than the right, because it has been trained to it.
What stands in the way of the work becomes part of the work. The obstacle on the road helps us along the road.
Do not be ashamed to be helped.
Stop talking about what a good person should be. Be one.

evening.t: From my grandfather Verus I learned good habits, and to keep my temper.
From my tutor: to endure hard work, to want little, to work with my own hands, and not to meddle in other people's affairs.

extra.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing. It must stand ready and firm to meet whatever comes, even the unforeseen.
Be like the headland the waves keep breaking against. It stands firm, and the water around it goes quiet.
Be satisfied with the smallest step forward, and treat that outcome as no small thing.
If a thing is hard for you to do, do not think it impossible for a human being. If it is possible for a human being and fits them, think it within your reach too.
Build your life act by act, and be content if each act reaches its end as far as it can. Nobody can stop you doing that.
Every hour, decide firmly, like a Roman and a human being, to do what is in front of you with simple dignity.
Let no act be done without a purpose.
If it is not right, do not do it. If it is not true, do not say it.
Your mind takes on the colour of your thoughts. The soul is dyed by them.
Nowhere can a person find a quieter or more untroubled retreat than in their own soul.
Do not let the future trouble you. You will come to it, if you must, carrying the same reason you use for the present.
If you work at what is in front of you, seriously, vigorously, calmly, without letting anything distract you, you will live happy. And there is nobody able to prevent this.
Let it make no difference to you whether you are cold or warm, drowsy or well rested, if you are doing what needs doing.
Attend to the matter in front of you, whether it is a thought, an act, or a word.

spoken.t: Good. You came. Sit where you are. The first one needs nothing but you.
You came back. That is the habit forming. The next one is ready.
That is the whole trick. You moved. Now the next one.
Five. Feel that? That is momentum starting. When I was a boy I boxed and wrestled and rode. Nobody becomes anything sitting still.

Ten, and you have not skipped one. These were made easy on purpose, so there was nothing in the way but you, and you moved every time. Most people watch their lives from the seats. You are on the field. Well done.

Ten done, and some skipped. I am not scolding you. I am asking: what were you waiting for? These were made easy on purpose, so there was nothing in the way but you. Every one of them shows you which you are: someone who acts, or a spectator. The two make very different lives. The ones you skipped are waiting at the end. Take them.
Fifteen. You are out of the chair, and I can see it in you. One thing from the room now.
Twenty. The last five are the ones people talk themselves out of. Not you. I am right here.
This one is a phone call. Thirty seconds. Everyone hesitates. Do it hesitating.
The last one. Ask about the house, or the car. They are there to answer. One minute, thank you, and it is done.
Twenty-five. Look at what you did in ten minutes. This is who you are when you move. I will be here tomorrow.
Skipped. Once is fine. It waits for you at the end.
Harder than it looked? Good. Those are the ones that count.
I am here. Take the next one when you are ready.
A stranger, out loud. That one changes people. On you go.
Read the tablet below, do what it says, then tap Done. That is all there is to it. If you cannot do this one, tap Not this one today, and it waits for you at the end.
The tablet below is the next one. Do it, tap Done, and I will be right here.
That is a breath between fives. When you are ready, tap Next five.
The twenty-five are done. Come back tomorrow and there will be more. Tap me again and I will give you something to think about.
This is for the ones who move. A spectacular life is here already, and most of it is free. It only has to be chosen.
Nothing here is difficult. Do one, tap Done, do the next. And do it. Some people tap Done without doing anything, to see what is at the end. Nothing is at the end for them. All of it is in the doing.
It takes one decision: to be that version of yourself, today. Ready?
I see it. It shows.
Good. That is one more than most people will do today.
Well done. See how little it took? That is the secret.
That is it. Small, quick, done. A life is built out of those.
Yes. Keep the pace. Do not stop to think.
You see? Easy. It was never about hard.
Ha. Good. You are moving now.
Strong. Another one behind you already.
Fantastic. The people who do these are rarer than you think.
Again, good. Momentum is a thing you can feel, and you are feeling it.
Lovely. Straight on to the next.
There it is. Done is a good word.
Better every time. The body learns faster than the mind.
There are two kinds of people, Aurelia. The ones who do the thing, and the ones who press past it, and miss the whole of life a few seconds at a time.
This one does the thing. Well done. Keep going.
Life is thousands of small actions, or thousands of small inactions. Nothing here was hard. It was only whether you would.
Most who begin a thing like this only watch it. A few do the first one. Fewer still do five. You are already in the small company that moves.
The ones people talk themselves out of. Not this one. I am right here.
Nobody great was ever made alone. Put high-minded people in one room, with someone to guide them, and what they build lasts thousands of years.
Almost none. You did, and you did it properly. That puts you in company most people never keep.
And if you tapped through without doing them, there is nothing on the other side for you. Not yet. The tablets are still here. Go back and do them.
Pick anything. The next thing keeps you moving. The long game is where you become somebody. Nothing here is out of reach.
That is one. The school is open, and you are in it.
A skill takes days. You just gave it one of them.
Good. Wide first, then deep. This is wide.
Three for today. Do one. If it is not the one, say so, and we will find another.
Fair. Here is another.
One for today, and the flame is lit. The school is yours. Go on in when you like.
Take one skill on. Some take an afternoon, some a month. A little most days is how the breath, the juggling and the language actually happen.
You have gone up. That is not a number. That is you, different from the person who started.
Most people never sit in a place like this. Now you have one. Stay as long as you like.
That is the whole school. Three buttons, one thing at a time, and the two of us. Go on.

tiers.name: Right where you are
tiers.line: Nothing but you, about five seconds each. Do not think about it.
tiers.lesson: Nothing to fetch and nothing to decide. The whole school starts with whether you will move at all, and most people never do. Five things, about five seconds each. Go.

quote.t: Well done is better than well said.

tiers.name: Still where you are
tiers.line: Half a minute each. Nothing to fetch and nowhere to go.
tiers.lesson: You will reach for a reason not to. Nothing to write with. Can't hold it that long. The lesson of these five is: find a way. A finger on the table counts. Half of it counts. Starting counts.

quote.t: Practise even the things you despair of. The left hand, useless at most things for want of practice, holds the reins better than the right, because it has been trained to it.

tiers.name: On your feet
tiers.line: Stand up. All of these are in the room you are already in.
tiers.lesson: The body goes first and the mind follows it. Marcus wrestled and boxed as a boy. Jefferson told his nephew to give two hours a day to it. Stand up. Everything here is in the room you are already in.

quote.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing. It must stand ready and firm to meet whatever comes, even the unforeseen.

tiers.name: One thing to find
tiers.line: Whatever is already in the room with you. Nowhere else to go and looking.
tiers.lesson: No ball. No pen. The wrong kind of paper. This tier is made of excuses, and every one has an answer already in the room with you: a rolled sock, a scrunched page, a finger, a stone. Resourceful is not a talent. It is a habit, and it starts here.

quote.t: Every habit and every ability is kept and grown by the matching action. Walking, by walking. Running, by running.

tiers.name: Out loud, and out into the world
tiers.line: Nobody else has to be there. The last two are phone calls, and if nobody answers, ring the next one.
tiers.lesson: The last five have other people in them, and the last two are phone calls. Nothing in them is hard. What stops people is a feeling, and the feeling is made of paper. Walk through it once and it stays walked through.

quote.t: It is not things that trouble us, but our judgements about things.

moves.test: Tap three times with your left hand, then three times with your right, on whatever is in front of you.
moves.fallback: Table, knee, book, the arm of the chair. Anything.

moves.test: Sit up straight, shoulders back, and take one slow breath all the way in and all the way out.
moves.fallback: Back hurts? Do it lying down.

moves.test: Say your own name out loud. Once. Actually out loud.
moves.fallback: Whisper it if there are people about. Out loud still means out loud.

moves.test: Reach both arms straight up, as high as they will go, until it pulls.
moves.fallback: From the chair is fine. Reach until it pulls.

moves.test: Stand up, and sit back down again.
moves.fallback: Hands on the arms of the chair if you need them. Once is enough.

moves.test: Write your name with your other hand. A finger on the table will do if there is nothing to write with.
moves.fallback: Nothing to write with? A finger on the table. A stick in the dirt. Your finger in the air.

moves.test: Close your eyes and count slowly to thirty. Slowly.
moves.fallback: Lose count? Start again from wherever you think you were. Slow is the point.

moves.test: Hold your breath for thirty seconds, sitting still.
moves.fallback: Can't manage thirty? Do the longest you can, and that is your number.

moves.test: Hum one note, and hold it for five seconds.
moves.fallback: Any note. Quietly is fine. Five seconds, then stop.

moves.test: Sit completely still and completely quiet for one minute.
moves.fallback: Fidgeted? That was still the minute. Count it.

moves.test: Stand on one leg for thirty seconds. Then the other one.
moves.fallback: One finger on the wall or a chair. Still counts.

moves.test: Two proper press-ups. Knees on the floor is fine.
moves.fallback: Knees down is a press-up. Against the wall is a press-up.

moves.test: Five sit-ups.
moves.fallback: Lying down and lifting your head is one. Five of those.

moves.test: Scrunch any paper into a ball and throw it into a bin from five paces.
moves.fallback: No bin? A box, a bag, a bowl, a circle of shoes on the floor.

moves.test: Fold a paper aeroplane that flies across the room.
moves.fallback: Any paper. A receipt, a page from a notebook, the back of an envelope.

moves.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand, ten times, without dropping it.
moves.fallback: No ball? Roll a sock. Scrunch a page. An orange. A bunch of keys.

moves.test: Draw something well enough that somebody would know what it is without being told.
moves.fallback: Nothing to draw with? A finger in flour, a stick in soil, your finger on a steamed-up window.

moves.test: Stack any three things you can reach without standing up, so they balance on their own for three seconds.
moves.fallback: A cup on a book on a phone. A remote on a mug. Three seconds.

moves.test: Tie a knot in anything within reach that has two ends — a shoelace, a hair tie, a charger cable, a sock.
moves.fallback: A shoelace, a hair tie, a charger cable, the belt of a dressing gown.

moves.test: Find something round and something square, both within reach, and hold one in each hand.
moves.fallback: A coin and a book. A lid and a box. An apple and a phone.

moves.test: Learn one usable sentence of another language, and say it out loud until it flows.
moves.fallback: One you already half know is fine. Where is the station, in anything.

moves.test: Sing one line of any song, out loud, at full voice.
moves.fallback: Any song. The first line of the first one you think of. Alone in the room is perfect.

moves.test: Look yourself in the eye in a mirror for thirty seconds. Then say, out loud: I am the kind of person who does the thing.
moves.fallback: No mirror? The black screen of your phone, or the selfie camera. Thirty seconds, then say it.

moves.test: Ring a shop or a cafe and ask what time they close.
moves.fallback: Any shop. If it goes to voicemail, that counts. Ring the next one.

moves.test: Ring somewhere prestigious. A luxury car dealer: do they do test drives? An estate agent with the grandest house in their window: is it still available? One minute. Thank you. Hang up.
moves.fallback: You do not have to want it. It is the same call as the corner shop, and that is the point. They exist to answer exactly this.

story.title: The boy who loved to wrestle
story.t: Marcus grew up in Rome, and loved wrestling, boxing, running and riding. The emperor Hadrian is said to have given him a nickname: Verissimus, the most truthful.

story.title: The emperor in a tent
story.t: He was made emperor at thirty-nine. He spent years of it not in a palace but in a tent by the river Danube, with the army.

story.title: Notes to himself
story.t: At night, in that tent, he wrote notes to himself in a little book, about how to be a good person the next day. Nobody was ever meant to read them.

story.title: The first page
story.t: The very first page of that book is a list of everyone who taught him something, thanked one by one. His grandfather, for good habits and a held temper. His tutor, for working with his own hands and wanting little.

story.title: The book that survived
story.t: The book outlived him by eighteen hundred years. We call it the Meditations. Every word Marcus says to you here is taken from it, put into modern English. Nothing else is ever put in his mouth.

voice.first: He is here. Tap him any time and he will speak.
voice.deck: Twenty-five in one sitting. You tapped, breathed, stood, threw, drew, sang, looked yourself in the eye and rang two shops. More action than most people take in a month, and you can feel it. This is what Light School runs on, and from here it gets bigger.
voice.break-seat: Five done. You moved, and most people never do. The next five you can do right where you are. You might reach for a reason not to. Find a way anyway.
voice.break-chair: Ten. You found a way every time, and that is the whole skill. Now stand up. The body goes first and the mind follows it. Everything here is in the room you are in.
voice.break-feet: Fifteen, and you are up out of the chair. The next five need one thing from the room. Whatever you cannot find, something in the room will do instead.
voice.break-fetch: Twenty. The last five are out loud, and the last two are phone calls. If nobody answers, ring the next one. What stops people is a feeling, and the feeling is made of paper.
voice.intro1: Light School is for the ones who move. A spectacular life is here already, with nothing new needed: a walk, a park, a gallery, a building that has stood for centuries, a country estate open to anyone, the finest shop in town, the people you read about, who live near you and can be met. Most of it is free. It is a choice.
voice.intro2: The choice needs momentum. Twenty-five tiny actions, about ten minutes, from the chair you are in. Do not think about them. Do one, tap Done, do the next.
voice.w1: Welcome to Light School. Most people wait: for money, for time, for the right moment. Life goes past while they wait.
voice.w2: Choosing takes momentum. So we start with twenty-five tiny actions, about ten minutes, from the chair you are in. Tap either of us at any time, and we will have something for you.
voice.w3: Most people who start something like this only watch it. That is the whole gap: watching, or doing. Feel what momentum is like, and see who you are at the end of it.
voice.b15a: Fifteen, Marcus. Look at them. Out of the chair and moving.
voice.b15b: My son grew up in the loudest street in Rome, and I taught him myself. He was never still a day in his life. The world knows him as Julius Caesar.
voice.b10a: Ten, Marcus. And not one skipped.
voice.b10b: And this one does the thing.
voice.b10c: Ten, Marcus. A few were pressed past.
voice.b10d: The ones you skipped are waiting at the end. Take them.
voice.b5a: Five, Marcus, and every one done properly. Do you know how few people do that?
voice.b20a: Twenty. The last five go out loud, and out into the world.
voice.b20b: The Greeks spoke of greatness so well that Rome went out and built it. Speak less. Build.
voice.fin1: Socrates taught Plato. Plato taught Aristotle. Aristotle taught Alexander.
voice.t1: The historian Tacitus wrote that I took charge of my son's education myself, instead of handing it to someone else. That son was Julius Caesar. That is the whole idea of this school.
voice.t2: My house stood in the Subura, the loudest quarter of Rome. Greatness does not need quiet. It needs a start.
voice.t3: Keep going. I raised a boy who never sat still, and the world still knows his name.
voice.t4: Every one of these is small on purpose. The size of the step is not the point. Taking it is.
voice.d1: Twenty-five. Marcus, how many people finish a thing they start?
voice.d3: On the other side of this door is a whole world of people building a spectacular life without waiting for anything.
voice.d5: Light School takes people in by application. We choose who we bring in. Tell us who you are.
voice.godoor: Now go to the door. Tap it, and tell us who you are.
voice.cat-body: Body and movement. Juggling, skipping, upside down, breath, strength, speed.
voice.cat-wild: Outdoors and wild. Fire, finding your way, shelter, weather, tracks, wild food.
voice.cat-water: Water and boats. Swimming, cold water, rowing, sailing, fishing, rock pools.
voice.cat-fit: Fitness and strength. Press-ups, sit-ups, pull-ups, the plank, lifting, sprinting.
voice.cat-sky: Air and sky. Kites, rockets, planes, stars, weather in the sky.
voice.cat-mind: Mind and numbers. Tables, the cube, chess, memory, codes, puzzles.
voice.cat-words: Words and languages. A new language, reading, handwriting, poems, stories, signing.
voice.cat-speak: Speaking and people. Strangers, the stage, listening, hard things, humour, teaching.
voice.cat-make: Making and building. Wood, cloth, clay, drawing, knots, electronics, machines, code.
voice.cat-music: Music and voice. Singing, an instrument, rhythm, songs, whistling, reading music.
voice.cat-magic: Magic and performance. Card tricks, coins, sleight of hand, mind reading, mime, puppets.
voice.cat-food: Food and the kitchen. Knife skills, cooking, baking, growing, preserving, hosting.
voice.cat-money: Money and business. Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.
voice.cat-beauty: Beauty and buildings. Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.
voice.cat-classic: The classical mind. Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.
voice.cat-nerve: Nerve. Small brave things, done on purpose, until they stop being brave. The later levels are for older ones and adults.
voice.cat-deal: Negotiation. Almost everything is flexible — the price, the terms, the timing. Most people simply never ask.
voice.cat-belong: You belong here. Fine shops, grand rooms and expensive things — so you never again decide somewhere is above you.
voice.cat-home: Home and repair. Keeping a place, mending, tools, bikes, first aid, engines.
voice.cat-care: Care and kindness. Animals, younger ones, older people, giving, the community.
voice.cat-calm: Focus and calm. Stillness, attention, sleep, cold, gratitude, doing hard things.
voice.s1: This is the school. Everything in here is yours now. Small things to keep the momentum, long things that take days and make you someone, and all of it laid out to be seen.
voice.a1: Welcome back. Here is where you stand.
voice.a0: You are in. The school is open, and it starts the way everything here starts: with one small thing done today.
voice.read-thousand: A hard thing is never one big thing. It is a thousand small ones, done so often that you stopped noticing you were doing them. The person who can hold a difficult conversation has had ten thousand easy ones first. So the steps that look too small to bother with are not the warm-up before the real thing. They are the real thing, arriving early and in pieces.
voice.read-gap: The question was never whether you can do these. Almost anybody can. What is being trained is the gap between reading one and starting it. Today that gap might be a day long. In a month it can be four seconds. Nothing else in this app matters as much as that number coming down, because every good thing you ever do sits on the other side of it.
voice.read-width: You cannot know what you love until you have tried it. Somebody does a voice warm-up for thirty mornings and finds out they love singing, and they would never have found out any other way. So the first job is width. Level one in as many things as take your fancy, including the ones that do not sound like you. The few you keep going back to are the ones worth going deep in.
voice.read-levelone: There is no age on any of this. A grandmother and a five-year-old both start at level one in juggling, and the grandmother is not further along for having lived longer. That is not a kindness we are extending to children. It is simply true, and most places pretend otherwise. Here the ladder is the same ladder, and the only thing that moves you up it is doing the thing.
voice.read-watching: Most of what looks like support is delegation. We decide the learning is for the children, and we take the chair, and we watch and encourage and ask how it went, and call that being involved. It is not. The thing that works is simpler and much harder: let them see you being a beginner. A child who watches a grown-up be bad at something learns something that cannot be told to them.
voice.read-sock: This is where people go looking for a reason to stop. No ball. No paper. Nothing in the house. But a rolled-up sock is a ball, and yesterday's junk mail is a paper aeroplane, and the sock you are already wearing is nearer than the drawer. The one who gets things done is not the one with the right equipment. It is the one who stopped hunting for the missing piece and used what was in front of them.
voice.read-checking: There is no inspector here. The only person who ever finds out whether you really did these is you, and you find out much later, on something far harder, when you reach for a skill you ticked and it is not there. Which means every tick is a small private promise. Keep them and the app becomes a true record. Break them and it becomes a decoration.
voice.read-supposing: Almost everything in your head arrived because somebody said it. Very little of it did you check. That is not a failing, it is how a person gets through a week. But it is worth knowing which pile a thing is in. Try it on something small today. Pick one thing you are sure of and ask: did I verify this, or was I told it? Both answers are fine. Not knowing which is the problem.
voice.read-askingno: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused. It sounds like a strange thing to practise. But most of what a person never gets, they never asked for, and the reason they never asked was a picture in their head of how bad the no would feel. Collect a few real ones and the picture corrects itself. After that you ask easily, and a great many things turn out to be available.
voice.read-backwards: There are eight hundred and fifty-two things in here and you will not do them all, and if you measure yourself against the pile you will feel behind for years. So do not face that way. Face the other way and look at where you were standing in January. That distance is real, it is yours, and nobody can take it back off you. The pile ahead is a menu, not a debt.
voice.read-nothingresets: You will miss days. You will miss a fortnight. Some apps punish that, and they punish it on purpose, because fear keeps people opening them. We will not do that. Days lit only ever goes up. A track you put down for a year is exactly where you left it, at exactly the level you reached. Come back on any day you like and nothing has been taken.
voice.read-emptyminute: Standing on one leg for a minute is a minute of nothing happening. Most people fill it with a screen. Try leaving it empty instead. The mind does something interesting when it is bored and cannot escape: it starts making things. Nearly every idea a person is proud of arrived in a dull minute, not a busy one. So the boring parts of these are not waste. They are the part where you get to think.
voice.read-beginner: Nobody is bad at things in front of other people any more. We practise in private and appear finished. It looks like modesty and it costs an enormous amount, because the fear of looking foolish quietly rules out every skill you did not happen to learn as a child. So be visibly bad at one thing this week, in front of one person. The fear is smaller than it looks from here.
voice.read-showing: A thing you can do alone and a thing you can do while somebody watches are two different skills, and only the second one is any use when it matters. That is why so many steps end with another person in them. Not to test you. Because the watching changes the doing, and the version of you that works under a pair of eyes is the version that turns up on the day.
voice.read-teachit: The fastest way to finish learning something is to hand it to somebody else while it is still wobbly in your own hands. You find the holes immediately, because they ask about exactly the parts you skipped. Learn a knot on Monday, teach it on Tuesday, and by Wednesday it is yours for good. A younger child is the best audience for this. They ask better questions than adults do.
voice.read-comparison: Somebody in this group will be ahead of you in the thing you care most about. That is worth being glad about rather than sore about, and here is the practical reason: they are the map. Everything they did, you can ask about. A person further along is the cheapest teaching there is, and the only cost is being willing to be the one who is behind for a while.
voice.read-speed: There is a habit of saving yourself for the difficult things. It feels like good sense. Then the difficult thing arrives, and there has been no practice at starting, only at waiting. Whatever you are going to do today, the best version of it begins now and badly rather than later and well, because later and well is a thing people describe and rarely do.
voice.read-hands: Almost nothing you own was made by anybody you have met. That is new, and it is only about a hundred years old. A person who can make one real object, badly, has a different relationship with everything else in the room. They look at a chair and see decisions. Sand one piece of wood properly smooth and you will understand what is meant by that.
voice.read-money: Money is treated as a mystery, or as something you either have or do not. It is neither. It is a set of ordinary skills: naming what a thing is worth, asking for a better price, being willing to walk away, doing one job well enough to be paid for it. Every one of those is on a ladder in here, and every one of them starts at a level a child can pass.
voice.read-beautiful: Find one beautiful thing today and say out loud why it is. Not a nice thing, not a pretty thing. Say the reason. Most people go a whole week without naming one, and then wonder why the week felt grey. The looking is a skill and it improves fast, and once it is working the world does not get any better. You just start receiving what was already there.
voice.read-courage: Courage is talked about as a quality, as though a person either has it in them or does not. Watch it closely and it looks much more ordinary than that. It is a thing that gets easier with repetition, in the same way that a press-up does. Ask for one small thing today and it costs you something. Ask for one small thing every week for a year and it costs you nothing at all.
voice.read-attention: Ten minutes on one thing with nothing else happening is now a rare event in most lives, and it is the exact condition under which anything difficult gets learned. Nobody has ever learned a hard thing while glancing away every forty seconds. The good news is that attention comes back quickly when you give it somewhere to go. Ten minutes is enough to start.
voice.read-failure: You will drop the balls forty times before the cascade holds, and every one of those drops tells you something about your throw that watching a video never would. This is worth remembering when a step goes badly. Nothing has gone wrong. You have simply bought information at the only price it is ever sold for, which is trying it and getting it wrong.
voice.read-curiosity: Ask why about one thing, and you get an answer. Ask why about the answer, and it gets more interesting. Ask a third time and you usually arrive somewhere nobody in the room has thought about before, including whoever you are asking. Three is roughly where the ready-made answers run out. Everything past that is your own thinking, and it is the cheapest journey available to anybody.
voice.read-family: This is not a set of activities for children while the grown-ups wait outside. When there is more than one name on this screen and one of them is yours, something changes in the house: the learning stops being a thing that is done to the small people and becomes a thing everybody is inside. That is the part almost nobody does, and it is the part that works.
voice.read-school: The word school comes from a Greek word, scholé, and it did not mean lessons. It meant free time. The hours that were yours, once the necessary work was finished, to spend on whatever a person would choose to think about. That is a strange thing to learn about a word most people associate with the opposite. It is also worth taking seriously, because it tells you what this was originally for.
voice.read-rest: Whatever you practised today gets filed tonight. That is not a figure of speech about tiredness, it is the ordinary way a body handles a new skill: you do it badly, you sleep, and it is slightly better in the morning without any further effort from you. Which makes going to bed properly part of the practice rather than the thing that interrupts it.
voice.read-gratitude: There is a difference between noticing something good and saying it. Noticing lasts a second. Saying it out loud puts it in the room, where somebody else gets it too, and where you hear your own voice make the claim. Do that once a day and the week reads differently by Friday. Not because the week changed. Because you kept a record of the parts that were already good.
voice.read-opinions: There is a track in here called not minding what people think, and it is one of the strangest ones to start, because the first step is deliberately looking a bit odd in public. The point is not to become someone who ignores everybody. It is to find out, once, first-hand, how little actually happens. Most people never test it, and so they carry a fear that has never been measured.
voice.read-wonder: The Plough is above your house tonight and it costs nothing to find it. So is the direction of the wind, and the shape of tomorrow's weather in the clouds this evening, and which way is north from your own front door. These were common knowledge for most of human history and are now unusual. Learning them back takes an evening each, and afterwards you are never quite in a plain place again.
voice.read-walkaway: Write down the number you will not go above, before you leave the house. Everything difficult about a negotiation is difficult because it is being decided in the moment, by a person who is standing in a shop and would rather not make a scene. Decide it in the kitchen instead, where you are calm, and then all you have to do in the shop is read your own handwriting.
voice.read-belong: There is a picture most people carry of which rooms are for them. Fine shops, grand buildings, expensive places. It is almost never checked, and it quietly decides where a person spends their whole life. So check it. Walk into somewhere you have decided is not for you and look at three things properly, without hurrying. Nothing will happen. That is exactly the finding.
voice.read-helping: Anybody can be helpful when they are asked. The interesting skill is noticing first: seeing the younger one standing on their own at the edge of the game, seeing the older person who would like to be spoken to, seeing the thing that needs carrying. That noticing can be practised like anything else, and a person who has it is welcome everywhere for their whole life.
voice.read-hardthing: Every so often, on purpose, finish something you wanted to give up on. Not a big thing. A jigsaw, a page, a set of squats. What you are practising is not the jigsaw. It is being the sort of person for whom wanting to stop is not the same as stopping. That distinction is worth more than any single skill in this app, and it can only be built one small stubborn finish at a time.
voice.read-sorry: A real apology has two halves and most people only ever say the first. Sorry, and then what you will do instead. Without the second half it is a feeling being described. With it, it becomes something the other person can rely on. This is a small mechanical thing, easy to learn at any age, and it repairs more than almost anything else a person can say.
voice.read-practice: Two hours on Sunday and nothing all week is worse than twenty minutes on six days, for almost every skill there is. This is inconvenient, because two hours on Sunday is easier to arrange. But the body files things overnight, and six nights of filing beats one. Which means the smallest daily amount you will actually do is a better plan than the amount you think you should do.
voice.read-names: Ten tools and what each one is for. Every note on a line of music. The parts of a small boat. Naming looks like the dull part, and it is the part that turns a blur into a set of separate things you can think about one at a time. Nobody can hold an idea they have no word for. This is why so many level ones in here are simply: name them.
voice.read-yes: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence, and give one good reason. That last part changes the answer more often than people expect. A request with a reason attached is easier to say yes to, because the person saying yes now has something to say to themselves about why they did. This is not a trick. It is simply how a reason works.
voice.read-ownway: There is no order, nothing expires, and no track is required. If a category does nothing for you, leave it entirely. The width is there so you can find what you love, not so that you tidy the whole thing up. A person who does forty steps in the two things that light them up has got far more out of this than a person who does one step in every track and felt nothing anywhere.
voice.read-excuse: Watch yourself the next time you decide not to do one of these, and notice how quickly a reason arrives. It is almost never laziness. It is nearly always an object in a different room, or a person not being available, or the wrong time of day. Which is useful, because those are solvable. Half of getting things done is simply seeing the excuse arrive and recognising it as an excuse.
voice.read-small: The first thing anybody does here is tap a table three times, and everybody who reads it thinks the same thought: this is too small to count. It is meant to be. Something that is obviously worth doing tells you nothing about yourself. Something that is obviously not worth doing, and that you do anyway, tells you a great deal, and it is the whole test.
voice.read-recordkeeping: In three years the useful thing about this app will not be the points. It will be the list of what you actually did, with the dates on it, when you have forgotten most of them. People systematically underestimate their own past effort, because the effort is invisible once it has turned into a skill. A written record is the only defence against being unfair to yourself later.
voice.read-weather: Half of the outdoor things in here get put off for weather, and the weather is not usually the reason. Dress correctly for what is actually outside, which is a level one in its own right, and rain becomes an ordinary condition rather than a cancellation. Children who learn this early get roughly twice as many days in their year as the ones who do not.
voice.read-onething: Everybody should be able to do one thing well enough to show it without warning. A card trick, a knot, a tune, a handstand, a poem from memory. It sounds like a party skill and it is not. It is a small solid piece of ground you carry into any room, and a person with one of those behaves differently in a crowd of strangers than a person with none.
voice.read-listening: Most listening is waiting. The other person is talking and we are assembling what we will say the moment they stop. Real listening feels different and it is noticeably harder: you do not know what you will say next, because you are still finding out what they mean. Try one whole story without being the one talking. It is a level one, and almost no adult passes it first time.
voice.read-repair: Something in your house is broken and going to be thrown out. Before it goes, take it apart and name five things inside. There is no risk, because it is already broken, and there is a great deal to gain, because most people go their whole lives believing that the insides of ordinary objects are beyond them. They are not. They are mostly simpler than expected, and slightly disappointing, which is the useful discovery.
voice.read-language: You do not need a language. You need one usable sentence, said out loud to a real person, and the feeling that arrives when they answer. That feeling is the whole engine, and it cannot be got from an app or a book, only from a person responding to a noise you made on purpose. Everything else about learning a language is a matter of repeating that.
voice.read-handwriting: Writing something by hand is slower than typing it, and the slowness is not a defect. A hand moves at roughly the speed a thought can be held, which is why notes taken by hand are remembered better than notes taken faster. It is also one of the few things a person makes every day that could be beautiful and usually is not, for no reason other than that nobody ever suggested it.
voice.read-argument: The commonest move in a losing argument is not a lie. It is a change of subject, done smoothly enough that nobody notices, usually to something the other person can be blamed for. Once you can see it happening, you cannot stop seeing it, in conversations and in speeches and in your own mouth. Noticing is the entire skill. You do not even have to say anything at the time.
voice.read-invite: Say hello first, before the other person does. It is a tiny reordering and it changes who you are in the room. The person who greets first is, from that second onward, one of the hosts of the situation rather than one of the guests in it. Children work this out very fast when it is pointed out to them, and most adults have never had it pointed out at all.
voice.read-onelevel: Every level in here is only slightly harder than the one before, and that is not a gentleness. It is the whole method. Progress stops the moment the next step is far enough away to require deciding about. Keep the next thing small enough that there is nothing to decide, and a person can climb an extraordinary distance without ever once needing to be brave.
voice.read-seasons: Width is for finding out what you love. Once you have found it, the opposite becomes true, and the useful thing is narrowness: two tracks for a whole season, gone deep on. A month of one skill looks slow from the outside and is the fastest thing there is. Choose them out loud, with somebody, so that the choosing is a real event and not a vague intention.
voice.read-first: Not the hardest. The first. Whatever the thing is today, there is a large gap between none and one, and a small gap between one and five. This is why the advice is always the same and always sounds too simple: do one. Not a session, not a plan, not a good start. One. The rest tends to follow on its own and does not need to be arranged.
voice.read-quiet: Sitting completely still and quiet for one minute is on the list of things that sound easy and are not. Most people last about twenty seconds before reaching for something. There is nothing mystical claimed here and no position you have to sit in. It is simply a measurement, taken on yourself, of how long you can currently go without an escape. The number goes up with practice.
voice.read-onthespot: Speaking when you have prepared and speaking when you have not are separate skills, and life mostly asks for the second one. The fear around it comes from imagining the room is judging the content. It is not. It is mostly relieved that somebody spoke. Say one unprepared thing in a group this week and notice how completely the room fails to punish you for it.
voice.read-fire: Gathering sticks that will actually burn is a judgement about dryness, thickness and species, made by hand, and it is older than every other skill in this app by a very long way. There is something worth feeling in that. Most of what we practise is a few hundred years old at most. This one connects you to every single person who came before you, without exception.
voice.read-swap: The picture of a good deal is usually one person winning. Watch the deals that actually last and they look different: both people walk away pleased, and both would trade with the other again. That second part is the valuable one, because a person who deals well is not the one who won once. They are the one everybody is willing to deal with a second time.
voice.read-map: Point at which way is north and be right. Find where you are standing on a paper map. These two are the beginning of a thing that most people never have, which is a picture in the head of where they actually are, rather than a blue dot moving on a screen. The dot tells you where you are. The picture tells you where things are in relation to each other, and only one of those survives a flat battery.
voice.read-cook: Cooking for yourself is a chore. Cooking for somebody else is something else entirely, and the difference arrives the first time you watch a person eat something you made and say nothing because they are busy eating it. Lay a table properly for everybody, once, and you will understand why so many of the good things in a life happen around one.
voice.read-photo: You have taken thousands of pictures and chosen almost none of them. Try taking one on purpose: decide what it is of, then arrange it so that somebody else could tell. It is a small discipline and it changes how you look at a street. The camera is not the interesting part. The deciding what it is of is the interesting part, and it costs nothing to practise.
voice.read-memory: People say their memory is poor as though it were a fixed size they were issued with. Memorise a six-digit number and say it back a minute later, then do it again tomorrow, and the belief starts to come apart. Memory responds to being used in exactly the way a muscle does. Almost nobody tests this, which is why almost everybody believes the opposite.
voice.read-youngerones: There is usually one child standing slightly outside the game. Bringing them in is a two-second act that they will remember for years. This is worth naming plainly, because it is easy to think of kindness as a large and effortful thing, and most of it is not. Most of it is noticing something small in time and doing the obvious thing about it.
voice.read-sums: Doing arithmetic in your head is unnecessary, in the sense that a phone will always do it. It is also the difference between hearing a price and feeling one. A person who can run the numbers as they are spoken is much harder to talk into a bad deal, and much quicker to spot a good one. Twenty single-digit sums in a row, correct, is where that begins.
voice.read-hundredthings: Juggling, and a card trick, and holding your breath, and lighting a fire from sticks, and a paper aeroplane that really flies. Any one of them is a novelty. Put a hundred of them together in one person and something different has happened: they see the world as a set of things that can be done rather than a set of things that are provided. That is what all of this is adding up to.
voice.r1: Nothing is asked of you here. Sit a while. The fire is lit, and we are not going anywhere.
voice.y1: Well done. That is one more thing you can do than you could this morning.
voice.y2: Good. See how the small ones add up? That is the whole method.
voice.y3: Lovely. Most people never take that step. You just did.
voice.y4: Yes. Another one behind you. Keep the pace and do not stop to think.
voice.y5: That is it. I taught a boy this way, one small thing at a time, and the world knows his name.
voice.y6: Done, and done properly. The flame stays lit for that.
voice.t-1: Three buttons, and that is the whole school. Next thing hands you one small thing at a time. The long game is for skills with a ladder: an afternoon, a week, or a month. Everything is every room, laid out to be seen.
voice.t-2: Where you stand: the days you have shown up, the things you have done, and your rank. The bar fills toward the next one.
voice.t-3: This is your next thing. Do it and tap Done. If it is not the one, tap Not this one and we find another. That is all there is to it.
voice.t-4: A flame for every day you show up. It never resets, and nobody scolds you. One light a day is the whole habit.
voice.t-5: And this is the portico. Nothing is asked of you there. Come and sit with us whenever you like.

cover.title: Light School
cover.tag: Seize the day. Build momentum. Craft a spectacular life.

what.title: What Light School is
paras: A school for people who choose to live at full strength now, not once the money or the time arrives. A spectacular life is here already and most of it is free; it is a choice, and the choice needs momentum. Its full name is the Nation of Light School. Everyone calls it Light School.

It starts with momentum: twenty-five small actions in one sitting, from the chair you are in, to prove to yourself that you move. Tapping, breathing, standing, throwing, folding, drawing, speaking, two phone calls. Most people never take that much action in a month.

Then the things that light you up get more of your life, and a small group and a mentor take you deeper. Behind the app there is a real community. The app is the way in, and the way in is the twenty-five.

deckQuote.t: It is not in the still calm of life that great characters are formed.

breaks.t: Five done. You moved, and most people never do. The next five you can do right where you are. You might reach for a reason not to. Find a way anyway.

scene.t: Five, Marcus, and every one done properly. Do you know how few people do that?
Most who begin a thing like this only watch it. A few do the first one. Fewer still do five. You are already in the small company that moves.

breaks.t: Ten. You found a way every time, and that is the whole skill. Now stand up. The body goes first and the mind follows it. Everything here is in the room you are in.

scene.t: Ten, Marcus. And not one skipped.
There are two kinds of people, Aurelia. The ones who do the thing, and the ones who press past it, and miss the whole of life a few seconds at a time.
And this one does the thing.
This one does the thing. Well done. Keep going.

sceneSkip.t: Ten, Marcus. A few were pressed past.
There are two kinds of people, Aurelia. The ones who do the thing, and the ones who press past it, and miss the whole of life a few seconds at a time.
Life is thousands of small actions, or thousands of small inactions. Nothing here was hard. It was only whether you would.
The ones you skipped are waiting at the end. Take them.

breaks.t: Fifteen, and you are up out of the chair. The next five need one thing from the room. Whatever you cannot find, something in the room will do instead.

scene.t: Fifteen, Marcus. Look at them. Out of the chair and moving.
My son grew up in the loudest street in Rome, and I taught him myself. He was never still a day in his life. The world knows him as Julius Caesar.

breaks.t: Twenty. The last five are out loud, and the last two are phone calls. If nobody answers, ring the next one. What stops people is a feeling, and the feeling is made of paper.

scene.t: Twenty. The last five go out loud, and out into the world.
The ones people talk themselves out of. Not this one. I am right here.
The Greeks spoke of greatness so well that Rome went out and built it. Speak less. Build.

finale.t: Twenty-five in one sitting. You tapped, breathed, stood, threw, drew, sang, looked yourself in the eye and rang two shops. More action than most people take in a month, and you can feel it. This is what Light School runs on, and from here it gets bigger.

scene.t: Socrates taught Plato. Plato taught Aristotle. Aristotle taught Alexander.
Nobody great was ever made alone. Put high-minded people in one room, with someone to guide them, and what they build lasts thousands of years.

godoor.t: Now go to the door. Tap it, and tell us who you are.

lines.t: Welcome to Light School. Most people wait: for money, for time, for the right moment. Life goes past while they wait.
This is for the ones who move. A spectacular life is here already, and most of it is free. It only has to be chosen.
Choosing takes momentum. So we start with twenty-five tiny actions, about ten minutes, from the chair you are in. Tap either of us at any time, and we will have something for you.
Nothing here is difficult. Do one, tap Done, do the next. And do it. Some people tap Done without doing anything, to see what is at the end. Nothing is at the end for them. All of it is in the doing.
Most people who start something like this only watch it. That is the whole gap: watching, or doing. Feel what momentum is like, and see who you are at the end of it.
It takes one decision: to be that version of yourself, today. Ready?

aurelia.name: Aurelia
aurelia.named_for: Aurelia Cotta, about 120 to 54 BC, who taught her son herself

lines.t: The historian Tacitus wrote that I took charge of my son's education myself, instead of handing it to someone else. That son was Julius Caesar. That is the whole idea of this school.
My house stood in the Subura, the loudest quarter of Rome. Greatness does not need quiet. It needs a start.
Keep going. I raised a boy who never sat still, and the world still knows his name.
Every one of these is small on purpose. The size of the step is not the point. Taking it is.

affirm.t: Well done. That is one more thing you can do than you could this morning.
Good. See how the small ones add up? That is the whole method.
Lovely. Most people never take that step. You just did.
Yes. Another one behind you. Keep the pace and do not stop to think.
That is it. I taught a boy this way, one small thing at a time, and the world knows his name.
Done, and done properly. The flame stays lit for that.

scene.t: Twenty-five. Marcus, how many people finish a thing they start?
Almost none. You did, and you did it properly. That puts you in company most people never keep.
On the other side of this door is a whole world of people building a spectacular life without waiting for anything.
And if you tapped through without doing them, there is nothing on the other side for you. Not yet. The tablets are still here. Go back and do them.
Light School takes people in by application. We choose who we bring in. Tell us who you are.

door.title: The door
door.lede: Light School takes people in by application. Tell us who you are and what the twenty-five did, and we will tell you what is behind each door.

fields.name: Your name
fields.felt: What did you feel by the twenty-fifth?
fields.which: Which door would you like to hear about?

which: I do not know yet. Tell me about all three.
Online, on my own, fully automated
Online with a community: calls, a group, mentors
A local community: families raising children together
door.codeLede: Members were given a code at the door. Enter it and the rooms beyond open.
door.codeSoon: The rooms beyond are being built. Your code is kept, and they will open here.
door.sent: Sent. We read every one, and we answer.

welcome.t: This is the school. Everything in here is yours now. Small things to keep the momentum, long things that take days and make you someone, and all of it laid out to be seen.
Pick anything. The next thing keeps you moving. The long game is where you become somebody. Nothing here is out of reach.

school.nextLine: Small, quick, doable now. Keep the momentum and try things widely.
school.longLine: Skills with a ladder: an afternoon, a week, or a month. One step at a time, the next one always ready.
school.allLine: Every room in the school, laid out to be seen.

long.intro: These are skills, not a sitting. Some take an afternoon, some a week, some a month of a little most days. Each one is a ladder: it starts small and ends somewhere you cannot do yet.
long.pickLine: The quick wins keep you moving. A skill gives them somewhere to go. Take on up to three, do a little most days, and put one down whenever you like.

lines.t: Welcome back. Here is where you stand.
Three for today. Do one. If it is not the one, say so, and we will find another.

first.t: You are in. The school is open, and it starts the way everything here starts: with one small thing done today.
Three for today. Do one. If it is not the one, say so, and we will find another.

room.title: The portico
room.lede: Nowhere to be and nothing asked of you. Sit a while with the two of them.

enter.t: Nothing is asked of you here. Sit a while. The fire is lit, and we are not going anywhere.
Most people never sit in a place like this. Now you have one. Stay as long as you like.

readings.title: A thousand small ones
readings.text: A hard thing is never one big thing. It is a thousand small ones, done so often that you stopped noticing you were doing them. The person who can hold a difficult conversation has had ten thousand easy ones first. So the steps that look too small to bother with are not the warm-up before the real thing. They are the real thing, arriving early and in pieces.

readings.title: The gap you are training
readings.text: The question was never whether you can do these. Almost anybody can. What is being trained is the gap between reading one and starting it. Today that gap might be a day long. In a month it can be four seconds. Nothing else in this app matters as much as that number coming down, because every good thing you ever do sits on the other side of it.

readings.title: Try a great many things, badly
readings.text: You cannot know what you love until you have tried it. Somebody does a voice warm-up for thirty mornings and finds out they love singing, and they would never have found out any other way. So the first job is width. Level one in as many things as take your fancy, including the ones that do not sound like you. The few you keep going back to are the ones worth going deep in.

readings.title: Everybody starts at one
readings.text: There is no age on any of this. A grandmother and a five-year-old both start at level one in juggling, and the grandmother is not further along for having lived longer. That is not a kindness we are extending to children. It is simply true, and most places pretend otherwise. Here the ladder is the same ladder, and the only thing that moves you up it is doing the thing.

readings.title: Do it beside them
readings.text: Most of what looks like support is delegation. We decide the learning is for the children, and we take the chair, and we watch and encourage and ask how it went, and call that being involved. It is not. The thing that works is simpler and much harder: let them see you being a beginner. A child who watches a grown-up be bad at something learns something that cannot be told to them.

readings.title: There is always something
readings.text: This is where people go looking for a reason to stop. No ball. No paper. Nothing in the house. But a rolled-up sock is a ball, and yesterday's junk mail is a paper aeroplane, and the sock you are already wearing is nearer than the drawer. The one who gets things done is not the one with the right equipment. It is the one who stopped hunting for the missing piece and used what was in front of them.

readings.title: Nobody is checking
readings.text: There is no inspector here. The only person who ever finds out whether you really did these is you, and you find out much later, on something far harder, when you reach for a skill you ticked and it is not there. Which means every tick is a small private promise. Keep them and the app becomes a true record. Break them and it becomes a decoration.

readings.title: Knowing and supposing
readings.text: Almost everything in your head arrived because somebody said it. Very little of it did you check. That is not a failing, it is how a person gets through a week. But it is worth knowing which pile a thing is in. Try it on something small today. Pick one thing you are sure of and ask: did I verify this, or was I told it? Both answers are fine. Not knowing which is the problem.

readings.title: What a no is worth
readings.text: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused. It sounds like a strange thing to practise. But most of what a person never gets, they never asked for, and the reason they never asked was a picture in their head of how bad the no would feel. Collect a few real ones and the picture corrects itself. After that you ask easily, and a great many things turn out to be available.

readings.title: Measure backwards
readings.text: There are eight hundred and fifty-two things in here and you will not do them all, and if you measure yourself against the pile you will feel behind for years. So do not face that way. Face the other way and look at where you were standing in January. That distance is real, it is yours, and nobody can take it back off you. The pile ahead is a menu, not a debt.

readings.title: Nothing here resets
readings.text: You will miss days. You will miss a fortnight. Some apps punish that, and they punish it on purpose, because fear keeps people opening them. We will not do that. Days lit only ever goes up. A track you put down for a year is exactly where you left it, at exactly the level you reached. Come back on any day you like and nothing has been taken.

readings.title: The empty minute
readings.text: Standing on one leg for a minute is a minute of nothing happening. Most people fill it with a screen. Try leaving it empty instead. The mind does something interesting when it is bored and cannot escape: it starts making things. Nearly every idea a person is proud of arrived in a dull minute, not a busy one. So the boring parts of these are not waste. They are the part where you get to think.

readings.title: Being bad in public
readings.text: Nobody is bad at things in front of other people any more. We practise in private and appear finished. It looks like modesty and it costs an enormous amount, because the fear of looking foolish quietly rules out every skill you did not happen to learn as a child. So be visibly bad at one thing this week, in front of one person. The fear is smaller than it looks from here.

readings.title: Say it out loud to somebody
readings.text: A thing you can do alone and a thing you can do while somebody watches are two different skills, and only the second one is any use when it matters. That is why so many steps end with another person in them. Not to test you. Because the watching changes the doing, and the version of you that works under a pair of eyes is the version that turns up on the day.

readings.title: Teach it the same week
readings.text: The fastest way to finish learning something is to hand it to somebody else while it is still wobbly in your own hands. You find the holes immediately, because they ask about exactly the parts you skipped. Learn a knot on Monday, teach it on Tuesday, and by Wednesday it is yours for good. A younger child is the best audience for this. They ask better questions than adults do.

readings.title: The only useful comparison
readings.text: Somebody in this group will be ahead of you in the thing you care most about. That is worth being glad about rather than sore about, and here is the practical reason: they are the map. Everything they did, you can ask about. A person further along is the cheapest teaching there is, and the only cost is being willing to be the one who is behind for a while.

readings.title: Start badly, start now
readings.text: There is a habit of saving yourself for the difficult things. It feels like good sense. Then the difficult thing arrives, and there has been no practice at starting, only at waiting. Whatever you are going to do today, the best version of it begins now and badly rather than later and well, because later and well is a thing people describe and rarely do.

readings.title: Made by your own hands
readings.text: Almost nothing you own was made by anybody you have met. That is new, and it is only about a hundred years old. A person who can make one real object, badly, has a different relationship with everything else in the room. They look at a chair and see decisions. Sand one piece of wood properly smooth and you will understand what is meant by that.

readings.title: Money is a skill
readings.text: Money is treated as a mystery, or as something you either have or do not. It is neither. It is a set of ordinary skills: naming what a thing is worth, asking for a better price, being willing to walk away, doing one job well enough to be paid for it. Every one of those is on a ladder in here, and every one of them starts at a level a child can pass.

readings.title: One beautiful thing
readings.text: Find one beautiful thing today and say out loud why it is. Not a nice thing, not a pretty thing. Say the reason. Most people go a whole week without naming one, and then wonder why the week felt grey. The looking is a skill and it improves fast, and once it is working the world does not get any better. You just start receiving what was already there.

readings.title: Courage is a practice
readings.text: Courage is talked about as a quality, as though a person either has it in them or does not. Watch it closely and it looks much more ordinary than that. It is a thing that gets easier with repetition, in the same way that a press-up does. Ask for one small thing today and it costs you something. Ask for one small thing every week for a year and it costs you nothing at all.

readings.title: One thing at a time
readings.text: Ten minutes on one thing with nothing else happening is now a rare event in most lives, and it is the exact condition under which anything difficult gets learned. Nobody has ever learned a hard thing while glancing away every forty seconds. The good news is that attention comes back quickly when you give it somewhere to go. Ten minutes is enough to start.

readings.title: A drop is information
readings.text: You will drop the balls forty times before the cascade holds, and every one of those drops tells you something about your throw that watching a video never would. This is worth remembering when a step goes badly. Nothing has gone wrong. You have simply bought information at the only price it is ever sold for, which is trying it and getting it wrong.

readings.title: Ask why three times
readings.text: Ask why about one thing, and you get an answer. Ask why about the answer, and it gets more interesting. Ask a third time and you usually arrive somewhere nobody in the room has thought about before, including whoever you are asking. Three is roughly where the ready-made answers run out. Everything past that is your own thinking, and it is the cheapest journey available to anybody.

readings.title: Not a programme for children
readings.text: This is not a set of activities for children while the grown-ups wait outside. When there is more than one name on this screen and one of them is yours, something changes in the house: the learning stops being a thing that is done to the small people and becomes a thing everybody is inside. That is the part almost nobody does, and it is the part that works.

readings.title: What the word school means
readings.text: The word school comes from a Greek word, scholé, and it did not mean lessons. It meant free time. The hours that were yours, once the necessary work was finished, to spend on whatever a person would choose to think about. That is a strange thing to learn about a word most people associate with the opposite. It is also worth taking seriously, because it tells you what this was originally for.

readings.title: Sleep is part of the work
readings.text: Whatever you practised today gets filed tonight. That is not a figure of speech about tiredness, it is the ordinary way a body handles a new skill: you do it badly, you sleep, and it is slightly better in the morning without any further effort from you. Which makes going to bed properly part of the practice rather than the thing that interrupts it.

readings.title: Say the good thing out loud
readings.text: There is a difference between noticing something good and saying it. Noticing lasts a second. Saying it out loud puts it in the room, where somebody else gets it too, and where you hear your own voice make the claim. Do that once a day and the week reads differently by Friday. Not because the week changed. Because you kept a record of the parts that were already good.

readings.title: Not minding what people think
readings.text: There is a track in here called not minding what people think, and it is one of the strangest ones to start, because the first step is deliberately looking a bit odd in public. The point is not to become someone who ignores everybody. It is to find out, once, first-hand, how little actually happens. Most people never test it, and so they carry a fear that has never been measured.

readings.title: The sky is free
readings.text: The Plough is above your house tonight and it costs nothing to find it. So is the direction of the wind, and the shape of tomorrow's weather in the clouds this evening, and which way is north from your own front door. These were common knowledge for most of human history and are now unusual. Learning them back takes an evening each, and afterwards you are never quite in a plain place again.

readings.title: Decide before you go
readings.text: Write down the number you will not go above, before you leave the house. Everything difficult about a negotiation is difficult because it is being decided in the moment, by a person who is standing in a shop and would rather not make a scene. Decide it in the kitchen instead, where you are calm, and then all you have to do in the shop is read your own handwriting.

readings.title: Rooms are for anybody
readings.text: There is a picture most people carry of which rooms are for them. Fine shops, grand buildings, expensive places. It is almost never checked, and it quietly decides where a person spends their whole life. So check it. Walk into somewhere you have decided is not for you and look at three things properly, without hurrying. Nothing will happen. That is exactly the finding.

readings.title: Before being asked
readings.text: Anybody can be helpful when they are asked. The interesting skill is noticing first: seeing the younger one standing on their own at the edge of the game, seeing the older person who would like to be spoken to, seeing the thing that needs carrying. That noticing can be practised like anything else, and a person who has it is welcome everywhere for their whole life.

readings.title: Finish the one you want to abandon
readings.text: Every so often, on purpose, finish something you wanted to give up on. Not a big thing. A jigsaw, a page, a set of squats. What you are practising is not the jigsaw. It is being the sort of person for whom wanting to stop is not the same as stopping. That distinction is worth more than any single skill in this app, and it can only be built one small stubborn finish at a time.

readings.title: The whole apology
readings.text: A real apology has two halves and most people only ever say the first. Sorry, and then what you will do instead. Without the second half it is a feeling being described. With it, it becomes something the other person can rely on. This is a small mechanical thing, easy to learn at any age, and it repairs more than almost anything else a person can say.

readings.title: Twenty minutes beats two hours
readings.text: Two hours on Sunday and nothing all week is worse than twenty minutes on six days, for almost every skill there is. This is inconvenient, because two hours on Sunday is easier to arrange. But the body files things overnight, and six nights of filing beats one. Which means the smallest daily amount you will actually do is a better plan than the amount you think you should do.

readings.title: Learn the names of things
readings.text: Ten tools and what each one is for. Every note on a line of music. The parts of a small boat. Naming looks like the dull part, and it is the part that turns a blur into a set of separate things you can think about one at a time. Nobody can hold an idea they have no word for. This is why so many level ones in here are simply: name them.

readings.title: The reason you give
readings.text: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence, and give one good reason. That last part changes the answer more often than people expect. A request with a reason attached is easier to say yes to, because the person saying yes now has something to say to themselves about why they did. This is not a trick. It is simply how a reason works.

readings.title: Nothing here is compulsory
readings.text: There is no order, nothing expires, and no track is required. If a category does nothing for you, leave it entirely. The width is there so you can find what you love, not so that you tidy the whole thing up. A person who does forty steps in the two things that light them up has got far more out of this than a person who does one step in every track and felt nothing anywhere.

readings.title: Where the excuse lives
readings.text: Watch yourself the next time you decide not to do one of these, and notice how quickly a reason arrives. It is almost never laziness. It is nearly always an object in a different room, or a person not being available, or the wrong time of day. Which is useful, because those are solvable. Half of getting things done is simply seeing the excuse arrive and recognising it as an excuse.

readings.title: Small enough to be silly
readings.text: The first thing anybody does here is tap a table three times, and everybody who reads it thinks the same thought: this is too small to count. It is meant to be. Something that is obviously worth doing tells you nothing about yourself. Something that is obviously not worth doing, and that you do anyway, tells you a great deal, and it is the whole test.

readings.title: The record is for later
readings.text: In three years the useful thing about this app will not be the points. It will be the list of what you actually did, with the dates on it, when you have forgotten most of them. People systematically underestimate their own past effort, because the effort is invisible once it has turned into a skill. A written record is the only defence against being unfair to yourself later.

readings.title: There is no wrong weather
readings.text: Half of the outdoor things in here get put off for weather, and the weather is not usually the reason. Dress correctly for what is actually outside, which is a level one in its own right, and rain becomes an ordinary condition rather than a cancellation. Children who learn this early get roughly twice as many days in their year as the ones who do not.

readings.title: One thing you can do
readings.text: Everybody should be able to do one thing well enough to show it without warning. A card trick, a knot, a tune, a handstand, a poem from memory. It sounds like a party skill and it is not. It is a small solid piece of ground you carry into any room, and a person with one of those behaves differently in a crowd of strangers than a person with none.

readings.title: Not waiting to speak
readings.text: Most listening is waiting. The other person is talking and we are assembling what we will say the moment they stop. Real listening feels different and it is noticeably harder: you do not know what you will say next, because you are still finding out what they mean. Try one whole story without being the one talking. It is a level one, and almost no adult passes it first time.

readings.title: Take it apart
readings.text: Something in your house is broken and going to be thrown out. Before it goes, take it apart and name five things inside. There is no risk, because it is already broken, and there is a great deal to gain, because most people go their whole lives believing that the insides of ordinary objects are beyond them. They are not. They are mostly simpler than expected, and slightly disappointing, which is the useful discovery.

readings.title: One sentence is a door
readings.text: You do not need a language. You need one usable sentence, said out loud to a real person, and the feeling that arrives when they answer. That feeling is the whole engine, and it cannot be got from an app or a book, only from a person responding to a noise you made on purpose. Everything else about learning a language is a matter of repeating that.

readings.title: Write it by hand
readings.text: Writing something by hand is slower than typing it, and the slowness is not a defect. A hand moves at roughly the speed a thought can be held, which is why notes taken by hand are remembered better than notes taken faster. It is also one of the few things a person makes every day that could be beautiful and usually is not, for no reason other than that nobody ever suggested it.

readings.title: Changing the subject
readings.text: The commonest move in a losing argument is not a lie. It is a change of subject, done smoothly enough that nobody notices, usually to something the other person can be blamed for. Once you can see it happening, you cannot stop seeing it, in conversations and in speeches and in your own mouth. Noticing is the entire skill. You do not even have to say anything at the time.

readings.title: Say hello first
readings.text: Say hello first, before the other person does. It is a tiny reordering and it changes who you are in the room. The person who greets first is, from that second onward, one of the hosts of the situation rather than one of the guests in it. Children work this out very fast when it is pointed out to them, and most adults have never had it pointed out at all.

readings.title: Only slightly harder
readings.text: Every level in here is only slightly harder than the one before, and that is not a gentleness. It is the whole method. Progress stops the moment the next step is far enough away to require deciding about. Keep the next thing small enough that there is nothing to decide, and a person can climb an extraordinary distance without ever once needing to be brave.

readings.title: Pick two for the season
readings.text: Width is for finding out what you love. Once you have found it, the opposite becomes true, and the useful thing is narrowness: two tracks for a whole season, gone deep on. A month of one skill looks slow from the outside and is the fastest thing there is. Choose them out loud, with somebody, so that the choosing is a real event and not a vague intention.

readings.title: The first one is the hard one
readings.text: Not the hardest. The first. Whatever the thing is today, there is a large gap between none and one, and a small gap between one and five. This is why the advice is always the same and always sounds too simple: do one. Not a session, not a plan, not a good start. One. The rest tends to follow on its own and does not need to be arranged.

readings.title: Sit still for one minute
readings.text: Sitting completely still and quiet for one minute is on the list of things that sound easy and are not. Most people last about twenty seconds before reaching for something. There is nothing mystical claimed here and no position you have to sit in. It is simply a measurement, taken on yourself, of how long you can currently go without an escape. The number goes up with practice.

readings.title: Say something unprepared
readings.text: Speaking when you have prepared and speaking when you have not are separate skills, and life mostly asks for the second one. The fear around it comes from imagining the room is judging the content. It is not. It is mostly relieved that somebody spoke. Say one unprepared thing in a group this week and notice how completely the room fails to punish you for it.

readings.title: Older than everything
readings.text: Gathering sticks that will actually burn is a judgement about dryness, thickness and species, made by hand, and it is older than every other skill in this app by a very long way. There is something worth feeling in that. Most of what we practise is a few hundred years old at most. This one connects you to every single person who came before you, without exception.

readings.title: Both sides pleased
readings.text: The picture of a good deal is usually one person winning. Watch the deals that actually last and they look different: both people walk away pleased, and both would trade with the other again. That second part is the valuable one, because a person who deals well is not the one who won once. They are the one everybody is willing to deal with a second time.

readings.title: Know where you are
readings.text: Point at which way is north and be right. Find where you are standing on a paper map. These two are the beginning of a thing that most people never have, which is a picture in the head of where they actually are, rather than a blue dot moving on a screen. The dot tells you where you are. The picture tells you where things are in relation to each other, and only one of those survives a flat battery.

readings.title: Feed somebody
readings.text: Cooking for yourself is a chore. Cooking for somebody else is something else entirely, and the difference arrives the first time you watch a person eat something you made and say nothing because they are busy eating it. Lay a table properly for everybody, once, and you will understand why so many of the good things in a life happen around one.

readings.title: Take a photograph on purpose
readings.text: You have taken thousands of pictures and chosen almost none of them. Try taking one on purpose: decide what it is of, then arrange it so that somebody else could tell. It is a small discipline and it changes how you look at a street. The camera is not the interesting part. The deciding what it is of is the interesting part, and it costs nothing to practise.

readings.title: Your memory is not full
readings.text: People say their memory is poor as though it were a fixed size they were issued with. Memorise a six-digit number and say it back a minute later, then do it again tomorrow, and the belief starts to come apart. Memory responds to being used in exactly the way a muscle does. Almost nobody tests this, which is why almost everybody believes the opposite.

readings.title: The one on their own
readings.text: There is usually one child standing slightly outside the game. Bringing them in is a two-second act that they will remember for years. This is worth naming plainly, because it is easy to think of kindness as a large and effortful thing, and most of it is not. Most of it is noticing something small in time and doing the obvious thing about it.

readings.title: Numbers in your head
readings.text: Doing arithmetic in your head is unnecessary, in the sense that a phone will always do it. It is also the difference between hearing a price and feeling one. A person who can run the numbers as they are spoken is much harder to talk into a bad deal, and much quicker to spot a good one. Twenty single-digit sums in a row, correct, is where that begins.

readings.title: A hundred small skills
readings.text: Juggling, and a card trick, and holding your breath, and lighting a fire from sticks, and a paper aeroplane that really flies. Any one of them is a novelty. Put a hundred of them together in one person and something different has happened: they see the world as a set of things that can be done rather than a set of things that are provided. That is what all of this is adding up to.

room.readingsLede: One thought a day. Aurelia reads it.

steps.t: Three buttons, and that is the whole school. Next thing hands you one small thing at a time. The long game is for skills with a ladder: an afternoon, a week, or a month. Everything is every room, laid out to be seen.
Where you stand: the days you have shown up, the things you have done, and your rank. The bar fills toward the next one.
This is your next thing. Do it and tap Done. If it is not the one, tap Not this one and we find another. That is all there is to it.
A flame for every day you show up. It never resets, and nobody scolds you. One light a day is the whole habit.
And this is the portico. Nothing is asked of you there. Come and sit with us whenever you like.
